territory.name: Puerto Rico
territory.summary: Ceded by Spain to the United States in 1898. Residents are U.S. citizens and elect a Resident Commissioner who cannot vote on the House floor. Below, each actor speaks in its own words, court and UN findings are kept separate, and every claim links to its source.

layer_rule: A perspective holds only that actor's own words. Court and UN determinations sit in findings. Scholarship and statistics sit inside modules, attributed to their producers.

modules.title: Legal foundation: from the Guano Islands Act to the Insular Cases
modules.summary: The legal category Puerto Rico still occupies, a territory that belongs to the United States without being fully part of it, was argued into place in 1901. One of the justices who built that argument cited the 1856 Guano Islands Act as earlier practice.

chain.text: The Guano Islands Act lets the President treat an unclaimed island where a U.S. citizen finds guano as "appertaining to the United States."
In Jones v. United States the Supreme Court upheld the Act and called islands acquired under it "appurtenant" to the United States, as later summarised by Justice White in Downes.
Under the Treaty of Paris, Spain ceded Puerto Rico (Article II), and "the civil rights and political status of the native inhabitants" were left to Congress (Article IX).

The Foraker Act replaced military rule with a civilian government: a presidentially appointed governor and executive council, an elected 35-member House, and a non-voting Resident Commissioner in Congress.

In Downes v. Bidwell, Justice White, concurring, cited the Guano Islands Act and Jones as government practice and concluded that Puerto Rico was "foreign to the United States in a domestic sense" because it had not been incorporated. Chief Justice Fuller, dissenting, rejected the guano analogy and objected that the theory kept a territory "like a disembodied shade, in an intermediate state of ambiguous existence."

The Jones–Shafroth Act made Puerto Ricans U.S. citizens and created an elected Senate and House, while the governor and the President kept a veto and Congress kept control of fiscal and economic matters.
Public Law 600 (1950) let Puerto Ricans draft their own constitution, which voters approved and Congress accepted in 1952.
General Assembly resolution 748 (VIII) accepted that the people of Puerto Rico had "effectively exercised their right to self-determination" and approved ending U.S. reports to the UN.

In Sanchez Valle the Supreme Court held that the "ultimate source" of Puerto Rico's prosecutorial power is the U.S. Congress, so Puerto Rico and the federal government are not separate sovereigns for double-jeopardy purposes.

notes.title: Name check: the "guano war"
notes.text: A different event is often called the guano war: Spain's 1864 seizure of Peru's guano-producing Chincha Islands, which Chile's government protested as an act of force and which led to war between Spain and Peru and Chile, including Spain's bombardment of Valparaíso on March 31, 1866. The sources used here do not connect that war to Puerto Rico's legal status, so it is noted here only to keep the two apart.

modules.title: Status plebiscites, 2012–2024
modules.summary: Four votes organised under Puerto Rico law in twelve years. None binds Congress, and the parties disagree about what the results show.

chain.text: Each plebiscite was organised under Puerto Rico law. The 2024 certification cites Act 165 of 2020 and calls the result a petition to Congress and the President "for a redress of grievances."

In 2017 the Justice Department declined to approve the ballot or release federal funds. It found the ballot "is not drafted in a way that ensures that its result will accurately reflect the current popular will of the people of Puerto Rico" because it left out the current territorial status. The legislature then added that option "under protest," and the Department did not formally respond before the vote.

CRS reports that debate centred on whether almost 500,000 blank answers to the second 2012 question should count, and that the legislature and PPD Governor Alejandro García Padilla called the result "inconclusive."

The House passed H.R. 8393 233 to 191 on December 15, 2022, with all 217 Democrats and 16 Republicans voting yes. It would have set a federally authorised vote on independence, sovereignty in free association, or statehood, with no status-quo option. The Senate did not take it up.

modules.title: Fiscal control: PROMESA and the Oversight Board
modules.summary: Congress created an appointed board with authority over Puerto Rico's budget and debt restructuring in 2016, citing the Territory Clause.

chain.text: PROMESA states: "Congress enacts this chapter pursuant to article IV, section 3 of the Constitution of the United States." The board is an entity within the territorial government and is not a federal agency.
According to the Board, when PROMESA was enacted Puerto Rico had more than $70 billion in debt and more than $55 billion in unfunded pension liabilities, with no legal path to restructure.
Judge Laura Taylor Swain confirmed the Commonwealth's Plan of Adjustment on January 18, 2022. It took effect on March 15, 2022.

The Board describes the plan as restructuring $33 billion of liabilities and more than $55 billion of pension liabilities to a sustainable $7 billion. AAFAF, the Puerto Rico government's fiscal agency, describes central-government debt falling 78%, from $34 billion to $7.4 billion, and annual debt service falling from $4.2 billion to $1.15 billion.

The Special Committee's 2025 draft says the Board exercises "plenary control powers over the elected executive and legislative officials" on fiscal and budgetary matters and notes the impact of austerity measures with concern.

modules.title: Nationalism and the Gag Law (Ley 53 de 1948)
modules.summary: From 1948 to 1957 a Puerto Rico law made advocating the violent overthrow of the insular government a felony. Accounts differ on how far it reached in practice.

chain.text: The Legislative Assembly approved Law 53 on May 21, 1948. It was modelled on the U.S. Smith Act of 1940.

It made it a felony "fomentar, abogar, aconsejar o predicar … la necesidad, deseabilidad o conveniencia de derrocar, destruir o paralizar el Gobierno Insular … por medio de la fuerza o la violencia" (to promote, advocate, advise or preach the necessity, desirability or advisability of overthrowing, destroying or paralysing the Insular Government by force or violence).

El Archivo de Borinquen describes the law as criminalising displaying a Puerto Rican flag, singing patriotic songs and speaking about independence. The statutory language quoted by Cumpiano Alfonso is framed around overthrow by force or violence.
After the 1950 Nationalist insurrection, the legislature amended the law to make mere membership in "subversive" parties a crime.

After the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in Pennsylvania v. Nelson (1956) and a report by the Civil Rights Committee, Governor Luis Muñoz Marín pardoned thirteen people convicted under the law on July 19, 1957, and asked the legislature, meeting in special session on July 29, 1957, to repeal it. The law was repealed.

Cumpiano Alfonso writes that the effects of "la mordaza" persisted after repeal, including lists of "subversives" kept by police. The Puerto Rico Supreme Court addressed those dossiers (carpetas) in Noriega v. Hernández Colón, decided November 21, 1988.

modules.title: La Operación: sterilization and population policy
modules.summary: By 1965 about one-third of Puerto Rican mothers aged 20 to 49 had been sterilized. Whether this was coercion, choice, or both is argued in the scholarship, and Puerto Rico's political movements took sides.

chain.text: Law 116 of 1937 set up a population-control programme modelled on U.S. state eugenics laws and authorised a Eugenics Board.

Harriet Presser estimated from the island-wide 1965 Master Sample Survey of Health and Welfare that about one-third of Puerto Rican mothers aged 20 to 49 had been sterilized, and concluded that sterilization was the main driver of the fertility decline after 1950.

Historian Laura Briggs describes competing nationalisms: the Nationalist Party opposed birth control and treated motherhood as the core of the nation, while many feminists, including some within the Nationalist movement, campaigned for access to birth control.

Ana María García's 1982 documentary La Operación presents women's accounts of sterilization. Anthropologist Iris López, as quoted by the Dig podcast, praised the film but said it casts the women as "helpless victims," and that in her research among Puerto Rican women in New York City, a woman who sought out the operation was more representative of the majority.

modules.title: Race and self-identification
modules.summary: Between the 2010 and 2020 censuses, the share of Puerto Rico residents who chose "White alone" fell from 75.8% to 17.1%. The Census Bureau, scholars and policy analysts give different explanations.

chain.text: The most common 2020 response was "White and Some Other Race" (38.5%), followed by "Some Other Race alone" (25.5%).

The Bureau says 2010 and 2020 race data "should be made with caution" and expects the national shifts were "largely due to the improvements to the design" of the race and ethnicity questions, data processing and coding.

Anthropologist Isar Godreau wrote in 2009 that the implicit goal of Puerto Rico's narrative of racial mixture is "whitening or blanqueamiento," and pointed to the 2000 census, when 80.5% identified as white and about 8% as black. Her 2015 book examines how national discourses about race "privilege whiteness, typecast blackness, and silence charges of racism."

CNE notes that the Bureau credits method changes while others credit changing self-identification, including campaigns urging residents to embrace African heritage, and calls the answer "an open empirical question."

modules.title: Hurricane María: the death count
modules.summary: The official count of 64 deaths was replaced in 2018 by a commissioned estimate of 2,975 excess deaths. A survey-based study gave a higher and wider range, and the President disputed the revised figure.

chain.text: Soon after the September 2017 hurricane, the Government of Puerto Rico determined that 64 people had died.
A Harvard-led household survey published in May 2018 in the New England Journal of Medicine estimated 4,645 excess deaths from September 20 to December 31, 2017 (95% CI 793 to 8,498).
The George Washington University study commissioned by the Government of Puerto Rico estimated 2,975 excess deaths from September 2017 through February 2018 (95% CI 2,658 to 3,290).
On August 28, 2018, the governor updated the official death toll from 64 to the GWU figure.

perspectives.heading: Puerto Rican nationalism under Albizu Campos

statements.original: Los imperios ocupan pueblos indefensos a cañonazos, a metralla, con gases venenosos o con vacuna, la cuestión es posesionarse de la riqueza del país y matar a sus habitantes.
statements.literal: Empires occupy defenceless peoples with cannon fire, with grapeshot, with poison gas or with vaccine; the point is to take possession of the country's wealth and kill its inhabitants.
statements.contextual: Empires take over defenceless nations with artillery, gunfire, poison gas or vaccination. What they want is the country's wealth, and they kill its people to get it.

statements.context: Quoted by philosopher Carlos Rojas Osorio, who cites it as "Acosta, 123." Rojas Osorio adds that Albizu believed there was a will to exterminate the island's population and denounced the federal government's Malthusian policy in Puerto Rico.

findings.text: Justice White, concurring: Puerto Rico "was foreign to the United States in a domestic sense, because the island had not been incorporated into the United States, but was merely appurtenant thereto as a possession."
